source.title: [Full Post] Progress Update #1 from the GDM Mech Interp Team

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cutoff; the text is a full post containing multiple research snippets.
record.tranche_reason: The inference-time-optimization snippet reports that changing sparse approximation while keeping a learned SAE dictionary fixed improves reconstruction loss, bearing on whether SAE reconstruction error can partly reflect encoder and approximation limitations.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are in the inference-time-optimization snippet. The post does not measure linear predictability of SAE error, cross-size token overlap, random-error comparisons, or downstream circuit and steering behavior for SAE error. Other snippets in the post are not relevant to the claim.
record.test_reason: Two snippets bear on versions, neither measuring dark matter directly. The ITO snippet fixes the SAE dictionary and swaps the encoder for gradient pursuit. Loss recovered rises markedly, so part of the reconstruction error comes from the encoder, a training or architecture artifact (V6). The steering snippet compares a wedding steering vector built from SAE reconstructions, with the error term excluded, against the original vector (V5). It finds the reconstruction a slightly worse steering vector. The post (April 2024) predates and is not the original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right for the ITO snippet. It should add that the authors find ITO 'significantly' improves loss recovered over the encoder, and that they do not yet recommend ITO as a drop-in encoder replacement pending interpretability study. It also omits the steering snippet's conclusions. There, SAEs can improve the anger steering vector (a single feature is a Pareto improvement) and partially interpret the wedding vector. However, the SAE reconstruction is a slightly worse wedding steering vector, and hand-picked features are much worse.
record.recipe_differences: Uses gradient-pursuit inference-time optimization with learned SAE dictionaries and evaluates loss recovered; it does not apply the dark-matter measurements described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Dictionary training L0 and target inference-time L0 affect the reported Pareto performance.

fits_no_version.finding: In the ghost-grads and Adam-beta1 snippets, SAE training techniques (resampling, rescaled ghost grads, beta1=0) shift the loss-recovered vs L0 Pareto frontier on GELU-1L up to Pythia-2.8B. Dark matter or the error structure is not measured.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction fidelity at fixed sparsity depends on dead-feature handling and optimiser settings during training.

fits_no_version.finding: A single SAE anger feature, used without the rest of the reconstruction or the error term, is a Pareto improvement over the original anger steering vector.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single SAE features can outperform raw contrastive steering vectors, so dropping the SAE error need not lose steering behaviour in some cases.

record.peer_reviewed: Alignment Forum post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The relevant Pareto results are described qualitatively without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. Interpretability of inference-time-optimized decompositions is not assessed systematically, and the post does not directly measure dark matter or separate its possible causes.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of SAE error from the input activation is not measured.
Per-token error norms across SAE sizes, shared failing contexts, and persistence with scale are not measured.
No comparison of SAE splicing against random errors of equal norm.
No split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts, and no test of which part further dictionary learning recovers.
Circuit analyses are not tested. Steering is tested only for one wedding vector in GPT-2 XL, plus an anger single-feature case.

The post does not show that dark matter 'mostly' reflects training. It does not test end-to-end training or new architectures beyond encoder replacement and training-technique sweeps. It does not separate linear and nonlinear error.

missing.what: The wedding steering vector built from the difference of SAE reconstructions (error term excluded) versus the original vector. It is notably worse at medium norms and slightly better at large or small norms. The TL;DR calls it 'a slightly worse steering vector'.
missing.locator: Activation Steering with SAEs, Section 4 ("The important SAE features for the wedding steer vector...")

missing.what: ITO with a random dictionary of the same size as baseline performs very poorly. This shows the gain comes from the learned dictionary.
A top-k test-time sweep confirms that a dictionary trained at L0≈100 beats one trained for L0 20 when used at L0 20.

Lewis Smith's author comment: gradient pursuit beat encoder-chosen top-k with reoptimised weights and beat a learned post-hoc shrinkage-correcting scale. So the gains are not just shrinkage correction.

record.verdict_notes: The post is a collection of snippets; only the ITO and steering snippets bear on versions. The ITO results bear on V6 indirectly, through loss recovered rather than error-vector analysis, and give no numbers. The steering result on V5 is recorded only in the text, so its verdict has empty row_ids. The anger single-feature result points the other way for V5 (no loss without the error) but uses a different operation, so it is listed under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is a linear function of the input activation.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, and whether error vanishes with scale.
Whether SAE-reconstruction replacement harms model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether the linear part contains unlearned features and the nonlinear part resists further dictionary learning.
Whether SAE-based circuit or steering analyses lose behavior when the error term is omitted.

The post tests the effect of replacing the SAE encoder's sparse approximation with inference-time optimization on reconstruction loss. It does not establish what share of dark matter is caused by training choices, test better SAE architectures or end-to-end training, or distinguish all training artifacts from structure in the model representation.

rows.subject: 1 layer model
rows.operation_detail: Applied gradient-pursuit inference-time optimization to fixed SAE dictionaries while sweeping the target reconstruction L0.

conditions.value: SAE dictionaries trained with different L1 penalties

rows.baseline: The original encoder with its corresponding dictionary
rows.value: Inference-time optimization generally leads to a significant improvement in loss recovered at a given sparsity level.
rows.note: The text describes the Pareto curves but gives no numeric values. The result shows that reconstruction depends in part on the approximation method used with the dictionary; it does not quantify how much of dark matter this explains.
rows.check: Measure is loss recovered after splicing, not error norm or a linear/nonlinear split. It shows reconstruction error shrinks when only the sparse approximation step is improved. No numbers are given, so the share of error attributable to the encoder cannot be read. A random-dictionary ITO baseline (performs very poorly) is a control not captured.

source_check.locator_found: Inference Time Optimisation, Empirical Results, lines 202–206.

rows.subject: 1 layer model
rows.operation_detail: Compared fixed dictionaries trained at different SAE sparsity levels using inference-time optimization at lower target sparsity.
rows.baseline: Dictionaries trained with lower L0, including an SAE trained to achieve the lower test-time sparsity
rows.value: The dictionary derived from the L0=99 SAE seems to have the best Pareto curve, including at low target L0; the text gives the example of target L0 20.
rows.note: The result indicates that dictionary-training choices affect reconstruction performance, but does not show that dark matter mostly arises from training artifacts.
rows.check: Shows the training sparsity penalty changes dictionary quality: the L0≈99 dictionary beats a dictionary trained at L0≈20 when tested at L0 20. The top-k sweep appendix corroborates this. This is evidence that training choices shape the error, but its size is unquantified.

source_check.locator_found: Empirical Results, line 204; Appendix: Sweeping max top-k, line 320.

rows.subject: Larger models and different activation sites (not specified)
rows.operation_detail: Compared inference-time optimization and encoder reconstruction across additional sites and larger models.
rows.value: The text reports similar results for different sites and larger models.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative statement; the post does not name the models or provide separate numerical results.
rows.check: A single sentence claims 'similar results for different sites and larger models'. Models and sites are unnamed and no values are given; it is very weak evidence.

relationships.condition: 1-layer model, post-activation (MLP) site, fixed SAE dictionaries with gradient-pursuit ITO; vaguely reported as similar at other sites and larger models
relationships.reason: Keeping the dictionary fixed and only replacing the encoder significantly raises loss recovered. Training L0 also changes dictionary quality. So part of the error is an encoder/training artifact (R1, R2, R3). Magnitude is unquantified, so this supports only the 'shrinks with better methods' part, not 'mostly'.
relationships.display_finding: Replacing the encoder with gradient-pursuit inference significantly increased loss recovery without changing the dictionary; training L0 also affected dictionary quality, but improvement magnitudes were unquantified.

source_check.reason: R1–R3 support a contribution from encoder limitations and dictionary-training choices. They do not establish that training artifacts explain most dark matter.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 XL layer-20-ish residual SAE, wedding steering vector reconstructed through the SAE with the error term excluded
relationships.reason: Based on the text, since no row records this. The reconstruction-only vector is 'notably worse' for medium norms but 'slightly better' for large or small norms. So the behaviour lost without the error is modest and norm-dependent.
relationships.display_finding: Excluding the error made wedding steering notably worse at medium norms but slightly better at large or small norms.

statements.problem: The norm-dependent comparison is accurate, but the wedding SAE's layer is not specified. Layer 20 is stated for the anger experiment. No numerical effect size establishes a modest loss.
